title: Epoxy mixing ratios: volume, weight and a repeatable sample
intro: A 1:1 volume ratio does not automatically mean equal weights. Build a mixing record around the exact formulation, measured quantity and working conditions before scaling a resin project.
materials: Current product TDS and Part A and Part B SDS
Graduated measuring containers or a suitable scale for the specified method
A batch record for temperature, quantity and observations
sections: Read the ratio and its measurement basis

Identify the exact resin and hardener before measuring. A ratio must say whether it is by volume or by weight. The supplied OS-820AB technical information specifies 1:1 by volume. Its two components do not become interchangeable with any other resin simply because another kit also says 1:1. Follow the instructions for the quoted formulation rather than a generic mixing chart.
Do not convert the ratio by guessing

Equal volumes can have different masses. If you want to use a scale for a system specified by volume, request the manufacturer’s approved weight ratio. Do not substitute equal weights, add extra hardener to accelerate curing, or estimate the ratio from the bottle shape. For a 2:1 by-volume system, two equal volume units of resin require one of hardener; that example does not establish its weight ratio.
Distinguish working time from cure time

Working time describes the usable handling window of the mixed resin under stated conditions. It is not the point at which the casting is ready to demold or package. OS-820AB lists about 35 minutes of usable time at 25°C for a 50 g mix and a separate 24-hour room-temperature cure reference. Batch mass, environment and geometry matter when translating test figures into a workshop process.
Make a batch record you can repeat

Record the product and lot references, measurement method, quantities of A and B, room temperature, substrate, mixing procedure and start time. Follow the prescribed mixing method, including the container walls and base. Note when application becomes difficult and when the piece meets the instructed handling criteria. Keep an approved sample with the record, rather than relying on memory.
Choose the resin around the application

A coating kit and a deep-pour kit should not share an assumed depth limit. For artwork and decorative surfaces, review the 1 gal coating kit. For a river-table cavity, measure the void and discuss the 3 gal deep-pour formulation separately. Send those measurements, pack requirements and estimated sets in your inquiry. Obtain current processing and safety instructions before production.
takeaway: Measure using the basis specified for the exact resin, then approve the process on a representative sample.

title: UV resin still tacky? Check the lamp, layer and color
intro: A cure time is useful only with its test conditions. Review wavelength, light access, layer thickness and pigment loading before changing a UV resin process.
alt: ArFlair 500 g clear UV resin bottle
materials: Current TDS and SDS for the selected UV resin
Lamp specification and the intended mold or finding
A small test piece and a record of layer thickness and exposure
sections: Start with the documented light source

Confirm that the resin and lamp are compatible. The supplied UV-3660 TDS lists 365–400 nm UV light and a reference intensity of 800–1,200 mW/cm². A lamp’s electrical wattage alone does not establish the irradiance reaching the resin surface. Ask for the applicable lamp and product instructions, and record the setup used for your sample.
Separate surface cure from complete cure

UV-3660 lists a 3–5 second surface cure and 60–90 seconds for complete cure of a 1–2 mm layer under its reference conditions, including a 20–30°C environment. These are different observations. A hard-looking surface does not by itself prove the entire piece is cured. Do not apply the thin-layer figure to a thick object or shaded cavity without validation.
Check where the light can reach

Review the actual piece, including its back, edges and areas under opaque inclusions. A deep cavity, hardware or decoration can limit light access. Follow the resin and lamp directions for layer thickness, positioning and any exposure from additional sides. If the proposed shape cannot be exposed adequately, discuss another construction method or resin system before making a batch.
Compare a clear control with the colored piece

Test the uncolored resin in the intended mold, then compare it with the proposed pigment and inclusion combination. Record what changes between the samples. Pigment amount, opaque particles and embedded decorations can change light access; do not assume a process that works for a clear pendant will work for a dark or heavily filled casting. Use only compatible additions and the product instructions.
Stop scaling until the sample is resolved

If a piece remains tacky or soft, treat the result as an unresolved process issue. Follow the SDS for handling, and do not package or sell it as a finished cured item. Send the product reference, lamp details, layer thickness, additives and exposure record to the supplier. For workshop planning, compare the 250 g, 500 g and 1,000 g packs after approving the same intended process.
takeaway: Validate the complete resin, lamp, mold and color combination rather than relying on a single advertised cure time.

title: Silicone mold sample inspection: detail, release and repeatability
intro: Approve a mold by casting the product you intend to sell. A useful sample review checks dimensions, detail, release and the finished result with the actual casting material.
alt: ArFlair silicone skull molds and resin castings
materials: Mold sample and agreed drawing or master dimensions
The intended resin or casting material and its instructions
An inspection sheet, photographs and approved finished sample
sections: Define what the dimensions describe

Distinguish overall mold size from cavity dimensions and finished casting dimensions. For a multi-cavity sheet, record the cavity count and compare each shape. Ask the supplier to clarify the measurement reference and any agreed tolerance before purchase. Do not infer finished-piece size from a photograph or assume a listed sheet measurement describes every cavity.
Inspect the details that matter to your design

Look at the features the customer will notice: skull teeth, animal toes, bookmark edges or hanging-hole posts. Inspect the sample for visible damage and unwanted surface defects. Photograph the mold and then the fully set casting under consistent lighting. Agree on an acceptable reference sample rather than using an undefined request for perfect quality.
Test with the intended casting material

Follow the casting material’s ratio, layer limit and curing or setting instructions. Resin, plaster and wax are different processes; suitability for one does not prove suitability for another. If candles are planned, confirm the mold’s compatibility with the specific wax process before ordering. For UV resin, include light access and the lamp setup in the review.
Review demolding and repeat runs

Wait until the casting meets its handling instructions before release. Observe whether fine details survive demolding and whether the finished piece needs acceptable finishing work. Repeat the intended process on samples and record the result. Do not turn a short sample trial into an unsupported universal mold-lifetime claim; discuss expected use and care for the selected design.
Approve the product and packaging together

List the mold configuration, included hardware, label, protective packaging, quantities and destination in the purchase brief. For a keychain kit, check both mold and hardware contents; for ornaments, review hanging-hole placement and any separately sourced cord. Keep the approved sample and a written checklist so incoming production can be compared with the same criteria.
takeaway: A sample approval should identify the exact mold, casting process and acceptance criteria for the finished piece.

title: 1 gal epoxy resin: a buyer's sample checklist
alt: ArFlair 1 gal epoxy resin and hardener kit
intro: Check the volume ratio, working window, substrate sample and pack details before ordering a 1 gal epoxy resin kit.
takeaway: Approve the exact resin, substrate and process before scaling.

title: Your first epoxy project: start small, make it yours
alt: ArFlair epoxy resin and floral coaster
intro: A small coaster is a useful place to explore mixing, color and finishing before moving on to a larger idea. Here is how to plan a first sample with fewer unknowns.
materials: An epoxy system suited to small castings
A clean, compatible casting form
Measuring cups, stir sticks and a level work surface
The protection specified in the product SDS
sections: Choose the project before the resin

Sketch the finished shape and measure its dimensions. A shallow decorative coaster and a thick block do not place the same demands on a resin. Check the selected product’s technical data sheet for its intended use, mixing method, batch limit and permitted casting depth.
Prepare before you mix

Protect the work surface and arrange every tool within reach. Keep the casting form clean and dry, and check that it sits level. Read the SDS and use the specified gloves, eye protection and ventilation. Keep the working area separate from food preparation.
Measure accurately, then mix thoroughly

Follow the exact ratio on your own product, including whether it is stated by weight or by volume. These are not interchangeable. Mix using the manufacturer’s method, reaching the sides and base of the cup. Work within the documented working time rather than trying to rescue a thickening batch.
Cast, protect and review

Pour within the stated depth limit and cover the piece against dust without touching the surface. Follow the full curing schedule before demolding and finishing. Record your room conditions, batch size and result so your next sample starts from something you can repeat.
takeaway: A successful small sample is a better starting point than a large, complicated first pour.

title: Small charms, bright ideas: a UV resin project plan
alt: Finished floral resin pendant, earrings and heart-shaped keychain
intro: UV resin can be a useful option for small decorative details. Plan the shape, light access and color together before you begin a batch of charms.
materials: A UV resin intended for your application
A lamp with the resin’s specified wavelength and output
Compatible bezels or light-transmitting casting forms
Small inclusions, a fine tool and suitable protective equipment
sections: Design around the light

Choose a small design that lets curing light reach the resin. Deep, opaque or heavily filled shapes can block light and leave areas uncured. Check the resin and lamp instructions together; a lamp that looks bright is not necessarily a compatible curing source.
Test the decoration

Try your colorant, glitter or inclusion in a small sample. Dense pigment and large opaque pieces affect light penetration. Start with a restrained design and stay within the supplier’s recommendations for additives and layer thickness.
Build the charm in controlled layers

Place the resin and decorations using the documented method. Cure each layer for the specified exposure, taking care to avoid skin contact with uncured resin. Shield eyes and skin from direct UV exposure and follow the lamp’s protective instructions.
Check before you assemble

Follow the manufacturer’s post-cure and inspection guidance. A hard surface alone does not confirm that the interior is cured. Do not package or wear a piece that remains tacky or has uncured pockets. Add findings only after the piece has completed its required cure.
takeaway: Resin, color loading, layer thickness and lamp compatibility all belong in the same sample test.

title: Build a resin color palette that works as a collection
alt: A coordinated range of original mica pigment jars
intro: A strong resin collection does not need every color. A few coordinated shades can make coasters, charms and gift sets feel connected while leaving room for individual expression.
materials: Compatible mica pigments or resin colorants
The resin selected for your project
Labeled sample cups and a notebook
A neutral background for comparing cured samples
sections: Give the palette a job

Start with an audience or mood: warm botanical gifts, cool coastal decor or jewel-toned holiday ornaments. Choose one lead shade, one supporting shade and a neutral. This creates a clear direction for packaging as well as finished projects.
Compare cured samples

The color in a pigment jar is not the final result. Resin type, casting depth, lighting and additive loading all affect appearance. Make small labeled samples using the intended resin and stay within its recommended additive limits.
Balance shimmer and transparency

Mica produces a different visual effect from a transparent dye. Consider where you want light to pass through and where you want a pearlescent surface. For UV resin, check how color loading affects the curing light before scaling up.
Turn the samples into a simple record

Keep the pigment identity, addition amount, resin formulation and cure conditions alongside each sample. Photograph the samples under consistent lighting. For a business collection, review these physical references with your supplier before approving a larger run.
takeaway: Approve the cured effect, not just a digital color swatch.

title: Six little keepsakes: planning a Christmas resin collection
alt: Original ArFlair Christmas resin kit and finished resin ornaments
intro: A tree, a star and a simple round ornament can become a coordinated holiday range. Let a small set of colors and repeated finishing details do the work.
materials: Resin appropriate for small decorative castings
Compatible ornament forms and fully dried inclusions
Resin-compatible colors or glitter
Ribbon, findings and protective packaging
sections: Choose a shared visual thread
Pick two lead colors and one accent. Repeat a detail such as gold flakes, dried petals or a ribbon color across the collection. Vary the shapes while keeping the overall palette recognizable.
Check the small details first

Make a sample to check the hanging hole, edge quality, weight and how the ornament sits on its ribbon. Confirm that the chosen inclusions are dry and compatible. Test any new additive with the resin before committing to a set.
Make a repeatable sample set

Use the documented resin ratio, depth limit and curing conditions for every sample. Record how much of each decoration goes into the design. Compare the pieces together after the required full cure rather than approving them one at a time.
Plan the kit around the project

For a DIY version, include a clear materials list and instructions specific to the supplied resin. Separate ribbons and loose decorations from bottles, and design packaging that protects both the contents and the finished sample used for display.
takeaway: A coordinated collection comes from repeated choices, not identical shapes.

title: A playful Halloween trio: pumpkin, ghost and a little sparkle
alt: Original ArFlair Halloween resin supplies with pumpkin and ghost crafts
intro: Build a Halloween story around three small decorative pieces. Warm amber, a soft violet and a clear glitter accent give the collection a playful character.
materials: A resin suited to the size of your castings
Compatible pumpkin, ghost or coaster forms
Resin-compatible color and decorative inclusions
Measuring tools and the required protective equipment
sections: Mix shapes with a purpose

Choose one statement piece and two smaller companions. A pumpkin, friendly ghost and round coaster offer different silhouettes while still feeling like a set. Plan the dimensions before choosing a resin formulation.
Keep the color story focused

Use a limited palette so the pieces work together. Compare a transparent amber sample with a light violet and a darker accent. Keep pigment and glitter additions within the selected resin’s documented limits.
Test visibility and finish

A decorative inclusion can disappear against a dark color or compete with a complex shape. Make a small sample to check the effect under ordinary room lighting. Review thin edges and detailed areas after the complete curing schedule.
Show the materials and the result

For a retail or wholesale presentation, display the resin and DIY supplies alongside a few finished pieces. The materials explain what is included; the finished examples help a customer imagine the project. State the actual kit contents clearly.
takeaway: Use finished pieces to explain the possibilities while keeping the kit contents clear.

title: Botanical castings: give dried flowers room to shine
alt: Botanical resin decor and floral casting
intro: A botanical casting is a balance of preparation, placement and material compatibility. Begin with a small arrangement before using a flower you cannot replace.
materials: Fully dried botanical materials
A resin appropriate for the planned casting depth
A clean compatible casting form
Fine placement tools and suitable protective equipment
sections: Start with dry, stable inclusions

Moisture in flowers can affect the result, and different petals react differently to resin. Select completely dried material and test a spare piece. If a sealer is considered, confirm that the resin supplier accepts it and test the complete combination.
Design the arrangement outside the form

Lay out the flowers on paper first. Leave enough clear space around the stems and petals so the composition remains readable from more than one angle. Check the finished depth against the resin’s permitted casting conditions.
Use the supplier’s layering method

Where layers are needed, follow the specified layer thickness and recoat timing. Place delicate flowers carefully without forcing them into a thickening batch. Avoid assuming that one resin’s layering schedule applies to another.
Evaluate the whole sample

After the required cure, inspect petal color, trapped air, clarity and the surface. Keep a record of the flower preparation and resin used. For keepsakes, make the test with expendable flowers before working with irreplaceable material.
takeaway: A compatibility sample protects both your design and the botanical material.

title: Epoxy or UV resin? Let the project guide your choice
alt: Epoxy resin product and casting application
intro: Choosing a resin starts with the object you want to make. Dimensions, light access, working time and the intended finish are more useful than a single “best resin” label.
materials: Your project dimensions and intended use
The candidate products’ current technical data sheets
A list of inclusions and colorants
A small sample plan
sections: Define the shape and scale

Measure the casting or coating and note the deepest section. Epoxy products vary in permitted batch size and casting depth. UV products depend on light reaching the material. A large opaque casting and a thin transparent charm need different approaches.
Consider the working process

A two-part epoxy requires accurate proportioning and mixing. UV resin needs an appropriate light source and a process that fits its documented layer limits. Compare how much time your arrangement requires before the cure begins.
Check the full material system

Include dyes, pigments, dried flowers, findings and the casting form in the review. Compatibility is about the whole combination. Ask for the correct TDS and SDS, then test the actual design under the recommended conditions.
Write a useful supplier brief

Share the dimensions, quantity, desired appearance, working environment and end use. Include photographs or a simple sketch. Request a sample recommendation rather than choosing from a product name alone.
takeaway: Select a formulation for a defined job, then validate it with a sample.

title: Before making a silicone mold: five details to settle
alt: Silicone molds and resin shape development
intro: A good mold begins with a clear master, a release plan and the right silicone system. Settle the design questions before measuring a batch.
materials: A clean master with a defined finished surface
A compatible silicone system and its TDS/SDS
A suitable mold box
Any sealer or release agent required by that system
sections: Inspect the master

Check the surface, fine details and undercuts. Every imperfection can transfer into the mold. Decide which faces need the best finish and how the finished casting will be removed without stressing thin features.
Choose the mold structure

A simple open shape may suit a one-part mold, while more complex geometry can need a multi-part approach. Plan the opening, support and alignment before choosing the box dimensions. Confirm wall thickness with the silicone supplier.
Test compatibility before the main pour

Some master materials, coatings and contaminants can interfere with specific silicone curing systems. Run the supplier’s recommended small compatibility test. Use a sealer or release only when it is suitable for the chosen materials.
Follow one documented system

Use the silicone’s exact ratio, measuring basis, mixing method and cure schedule. Check whether degassing is recommended for that formulation. After curing, inspect the mold and trial it with the intended casting material before repeating production.
takeaway: The master, silicone and casting material need to work together as one system.

title: From project idea to a private-label DIY kit
intro: A useful DIY kit helps a customer complete one clear project. Define that experience first, then choose the materials, instructions and packaging around it.
materials: A target customer and one main project
A provisional bill of materials
Packaging dimensions and label requirements
A sample review checklist
sections: Write the customer outcome

Describe what someone should be able to make and how many pieces the kit is intended to produce. Decide who the instructions are for. This prevents accessories from accumulating without a role in the project.
Build the bill of materials

List each resin component, decoration, tool and consumable with a proposed quantity. Check that the supplied resin quantity suits the project and its documented batch limits. Distinguish included items from tools the customer must provide.
Make the instructions match the contents

Use the exact resin’s current processing instructions and safety information. Illustrate the preparation, measuring, mixing and curing sequence. Have a tester work through the draft using only the listed contents and required extra tools.
Review the complete sample

Assess the finished result alongside bottle labels, leak protection, internal packing and the outer carton. Confirm quantities, artwork, commercial terms and the approval sample with the supplier before placing a production order.
takeaway: Approve the customer experience, not just the appearance of the box.

title: Clearer castings begin with better preparation
intro: Trapped air and uneven surfaces rarely have a single cause. A simple record of preparation and processing can help you find what to change in the next sample.
materials: A resin matched to the casting depth
Clean dry tools and compatible forms
Accurate measuring equipment
A sample log for the working conditions
sections: Control the starting conditions

Use the temperature and humidity range given for your resin. Keep tools, forms and inclusions dry. Check whether porous inclusions need a compatible sealing process and trial it on a spare sample first.
Measure and mix with care

Follow the exact ratio and measuring basis. Mix as directed while reaching the cup walls and base. Do not change the hardener quantity to alter the cure speed; that changes the formulation rather than correcting a process issue.
Keep the pour within its limits

Observe the recommended batch size and depth. If a multi-layer process is needed, use the specified recoat window. Use pressure, vacuum or heat only when the resin and equipment suppliers expressly support that method.
Change one thing at a time

After the required cure, compare where defects appear: at inclusions, along edges or throughout the piece. Record the conditions and alter one variable for the next test. This makes the result more useful than changing several steps at once.
takeaway: A repeatable process is more valuable than a quick fix for one pour.

title: Casting powder projects: plan the surface before the pour
intro: Casting powders can produce a different look from transparent resin. Begin with the desired surface, the shape and the exact material system before planning a decorative range.
materials: A selected casting powder and its product instructions
The specified liquid binder or water
Accurate measuring tools and a compatible casting form
A finish or sealer confirmed suitable for that material
sections: Identify the material first

“Casting powder” covers different formulations. Confirm the composition, binder and measuring basis from the supplier. A ratio or demolding time for one powder should not be applied to another product with a similar name.
Make a small working sample

Prepare the ingredients using the documented ratio and mixing sequence. Control dust as described in the SDS and use the specified protective measures. Keep the form on a level surface and follow the recommended filling method.
Separate demolding from final readiness
A piece that can be removed from its form may still need additional drying or curing before finishing. Follow the material’s full schedule and check when sanding, painting or sealing is permitted.
Test the intended finish

Try color, paint and a compatible sealer on a sample before approving a collection. Assess the result against the actual use; do not assume a decorative casting is suitable for food contact, prolonged water exposure or outdoor service.
takeaway: The specific formulation determines the process and the suitable end use.

title: A seasonal range, ready for review: your sample checklist
alt: ArFlair seasonal packaging and resin ornaments
intro: A seasonal sample should answer more than whether the collection looks good. Use one checklist to connect the product, packaging and order plan.
materials: A proposed product list and quantity plan
Physical color and finish references
Packaging artwork and kit contents
A written list of open questions
sections: Review the range together

Lay out the whole collection, including bottles, accessories and finished display samples. Check that the colors, names and pack sizes tell a clear story. Remove items that complicate the range without improving the customer project.
Check the practical details

Compare the contents against the bill of materials. Confirm closures, internal separation and how loose items are packed. Review instructions and labels for the exact material supplied, including the required safety information.
Connect the sample to the order

Record the approved version, artwork references and specifications. Ask the supplier to confirm minimum quantities, production timing, shipping assumptions and quotation validity. A photograph of a sample does not replace those written details.
Keep a record of the decision

Store the approved sample reference and a short list of any remaining changes. Assign an owner to each question before the purchase decision. Clear sign-off helps the collection stay consistent when it moves from a creative idea into an order.
takeaway: One documented approval reference keeps the product, artwork and commercial discussion aligned.

title: River tables & wood projects: plan your resin pour
alt: Walnut and amber resin river table project
intro: A river table starts with the wood, the casting dimensions and a resin system designed for the job. Plan a small test before committing material to a full tabletop.
materials: Dry, stable wood and a clean, level casting form
A casting epoxy documented for the intended pour dimensions
Compatible release and sealing materials
Measuring tools and the protection specified in the product SDS
sections: Measure the pour before choosing a resin

Record the channel length, width and depth, including irregular spaces around live edges. Share these dimensions with your resin supplier. Ask for the exact formulation’s permitted pour depth, batch size, working conditions and cure schedule; a general craft epoxy may not suit a deep river casting.
Prepare the wood and the casting form

Check that the wood is dry and stable. Remove loose material and prepare the surface using the resin supplier’s guidance. Confirm whether a compatible seal coat is needed. Secure the wood in a level, leak-resistant form and test the release method on a spare piece.
Make a representative sample

Use an offcut of the intended wood with the proposed resin, color and surface preparation. Review adhesion, bubbles and appearance after the specified cure. Approve the sample before scaling up, and record the material combination so you can repeat it.
Plan pouring, curing and finishing together

Follow the exact mixing ratio, batch limit and pour schedule in the current TDS. Larger pours can retain heat, so do not increase depth or batch size without supplier guidance. Allow the required cure before demolding and machining, and control sanding dust using the prescribed protection.
takeaway: Choose a formulation for the measured pour, then validate the complete wood-and-resin combination in a sample.

title: Resin coasters & trays: design a coordinated home collection
alt: Finished floral resin tray and ocean coasters
intro: Coasters and trays turn color, shape and small details into a useful decorative collection. Start with one sample design and choose materials around the intended finish and use.
materials: Casting material suited to the shape and intended decorative use
Clean, compatible coaster or tray molds
Compatible pigments and fully dried decorative inclusions
Measuring tools and the protection specified by the material supplier
sections: Define the finished piece

Decide whether you are making a transparent floral tray, an ocean-effect coaster or an opaque cast accessory. Record the dimensions, edge shape and desired finish. Select resin or casting powder for that specific result rather than treating the materials as interchangeable.
Keep the collection visually connected

Use a small palette and repeat one feature across the tray and coasters, such as a flower type, a rim color or a wave detail. Check that the mold dimensions and thickness leave room for the design. Test inclusions and colorants with your chosen formulation.
Cast a small sample first

Prepare, measure, mix and cure according to the exact product instructions. Follow the stated limits for casting depth, pigment loading and batch size. For powder casting, follow its own powder-to-water ratio and drying guidance. Inspect the fully cured or dried sample for bubbles, edges and surface quality.
Review use, care and packaging

Check the finished item against its intended use. Do not assume a resin piece is suitable for food contact, hot cookware or dishwashers; confirm documented suitability before making such claims. Consider protective feet, care instructions and packaging that keeps the surface from rubbing during shipping.
takeaway: A coordinated collection starts with a repeatable sample and clear expectations for how the finished pieces will be used.
